modules.title: Foundations & Scope
modules.desc: Build the inland-waterway mindset before learning individual rules.
sections: WHAT CEVNI IS

CEVNI is the UNECE harmonised code for navigation on inland waterways. It provides a common framework for vessel marks, visual and sound signals, radiotelephony, signs and marking, conduct of vessels, berthing, reporting and environmental duties.
CEVNI IS NOT COLREGs ON A RIVER

Inland waterways create different constraints: defined fairways, banks, locks, bridges, commercial traffic, local traffic systems and waterway-specific instructions. Do not assume an open-sea answer automatically transfers inland.
THE LOCAL LAYER

CEVNI is a harmonised basis, while national, regional and local provisions can supplement the framework. Before passage, identify the competent authority and the rules and notices applying to the actual waterway.
COMPETENT AUTHORITY
The competent authority is central to inland operation. Local instructions can govern matters such as traffic movements, reporting, locks, bridges, restricted sections and temporary conditions.
NOTICES BEFORE DEPARTURE
A good inland passage starts before casting off: check current navigation notices, closures, restrictions, works, lock information and any temporary directions relevant to the planned route.
READ THE WHOLE WATERWAY

Treat signs, bank marks, lights, sound signals, radio calls, traffic movements and physical restrictions as one navigation picture. One isolated cue should not override contradictory evidence around you.
EARLY DECISIONS

Constrained water removes options quickly. Identify the next restriction, reporting point, bridge, lock or traffic conflict early enough to slow, wait or reposition without creating a last-second problem.
PROJECT WATCH METHOD
Learn the rule, recognise the signal, place it in context, then apply it. The mock should confirm knowledge already taught; it should never be the first place you meet a subject.

modules.title: Vessels, Marks & Definitions
modules.desc: Learn the inland vocabulary and physical limits that change how rules are applied.
sections: WHY DEFINITIONS MATTER
CEVNI distinguishes vessel types, small craft, formations and particular operations because duties and displayed signals can depend on what a vessel is and what it is doing.
SMALL CRAFT

Do not treat “small craft” as meaning “outside the rules”. Inland provisions can distinguish small craft from larger vessels, but the skipper still has to identify and comply with the rules applying to the situation.
LENGTH, BEAM AND DRAUGHT
Length and beam affect available space; draught determines the water depth required. On a constrained waterway these are immediate passage-planning numbers, not merely specifications in the handbook.
AIR DRAUGHT

Bridges, cables and other overhead restrictions make air draught operationally important. Know the vessel’s actual requirement and compare it with the applicable clearance information and local conditions.
AVAILABLE WATER
A charted or signed dimension is not a reason to abandon judgement. Allow for the applicable water level, local information, vessel movement and any safety margin required by the situation.
VESSEL MARKS
Identification marks and draught information help authorities and other users understand the vessel. Learn to distinguish permanent vessel information from temporary navigation signals.
STATUS SIGNALS

Lights, boards, balls, cones, cylinders and other displays can communicate a vessel’s status or operation. The correct interpretation depends on the complete display and the context in which it is seen.
FORMATION AWARENESS
Tows, pushed formations and coupled craft may present a larger and less manoeuvrable traffic picture than one hull suggests. Judge the complete formation, not just the nearest visible bow.

modules.title: Signs, Signals & Fairway Marks
modules.desc: Learn the visual language of the waterway before being asked to recognise it under pressure.
sections: THE FIVE ANNEX 7 FAMILIES
A = prohibitory, B = mandatory, C = restrictive, D = recommendatory and E = informative. First identify what family of instruction you are looking at, then identify the individual sign.
A — PROHIBITORY
A-series signs tell you something is prohibited. Examples already in the verified library include A.1 No entry and A.2 No overtaking. A prohibition is not optional guidance.
B — MANDATORY
B-series signs prescribe an action. Verified examples include B.1 Proceed in the direction shown and B.7 Give a sound signal. The action shown is something the navigator is required to do.
C — RESTRICTIVE
C-series signs communicate restrictions such as limited dimensions. C.1 concerns limited depth. Numbers and symbols must be read as part of the restriction and checked against your vessel.
D — RECOMMENDATORY

D-series signs indicate recommended navigation. D.1 identifies a recommended opening. “Recommended” differs from “mandatory”, but it still carries navigational meaning and should be considered in context.
E — INFORMATIVE

E-series signs provide information useful to navigation. Verified examples in this build include E.1 Entry permitted and E.2 Overhead cable crossing. Information signs can identify facilities, conditions or permitted actions.
AUXILIARY INFORMATION
Main signs may be supplemented or clarified by auxiliary information. Never memorise only the central pictogram and ignore an attached panel, arrow, distance or qualifying information.
ANNEX 8 IS DIFFERENT
Waterway marking and buoyage are treated separately from the Annex 7 notice-sign families. Marking can define fairway limits, banks, hazards, obstacles and other features of the navigable waterway.
CONTEXT RECOGNITION
A sign should ultimately be recognised where it matters: on a bank, bridge, lock approach or fairway. Project Watch will increasingly test signs in a scene rather than as isolated flash cards.
ACTION SEQUENCE
See the sign → identify its family → read the specific meaning and any auxiliary information → compare it with vessel dimensions/status → act early enough to comply safely.

modules.title: Lights & Day Signals
modules.desc: Recognise visual information carried by vessels and infrastructure without guessing from one colour or shape.
sections: WHY VISUAL SIGNALS EXIST
Visual signals allow vessels and infrastructure to communicate status and restrictions without depending entirely on spoken language. They form part of the navigation picture by day and by night.
BUILD THE PICTURE
Start with what is genuinely visible: colours, number of lights or shapes, relative positions and aspect. Then identify the vessel or installation and only then attach a rule meaning.
ASPECT MATTERS
The same vessel can present a different light picture from ahead, astern or the side. Never assume a missing light is present merely because a particular answer would make the pattern convenient.
DAY AND NIGHT
Day shapes and night lights often communicate related operational information in different ways. Training should connect the day and night presentations rather than teach them as unrelated lists.
VESSEL STATUS

A vessel’s display may tell you more than its direction of travel. Particular operations, restricted manoeuvrability or formations can change what must be displayed and how you should interpret the encounter.
INFRASTRUCTURE SIGNALS
Locks, bridges and controlled passages can also use visual signals. Treat them as operating instructions for the infrastructure, not as vessel navigation lights.
NO SINGLE-CUE GUESSING
Colour alone, one light alone or AIS alone is not enough when the overall picture is inconsistent. Maintain lookout and verify before committing to an interpretation.
RECOGNITION DRILL
Project Watch method: observe → describe → identify → interpret → decide. This order prevents the learner seeing a familiar colour and jumping straight to an unsupported answer.

modules.title: Sound Signals & Radiotelephony
modules.desc: Hear, recognise and apply the inland sound vocabulary, then connect it with radio procedure.
sections: BLAST TIMING

For Project Watch recognition, a short blast is approximately 1 second, a long blast approximately 4 seconds and a very short blast approximately a quarter second. Hear the difference in Sound Lab rather than memorising punctuation.
ONE LONG
One long blast is the general caution signal in the material taught here. Train your ear to recognise the duration before trying to name the meaning.
COURSE ALTERATIONS
One short blast = altering course to starboard. Two short blasts = altering course to port. Keep the sequence tied to the actual sound pattern.
ASTERN AND UNABLE
Three short blasts = going astern. Four short blasts = unable to manoeuvre. These are different operational messages and should not be confused with the danger series.
DO NOT APPROACH
The short + long pattern repeated is taught in the Sound Lab as “do not approach”. Listen for the alternating short/long rhythm rather than counting only the total number of blasts.
IMMINENT DANGER
A series of at least six very short blasts warns of imminent danger of collision. The rapid quarter-second character makes it audibly different from a normal sequence of short manoeuvring blasts.
TURNING SIGNALS
One long + one short indicates turning to starboard; one long + two short indicates turning to port in the Sound Lab set. Recognise the long lead blast first, then count the short blasts.
HARBOUR / TRIBUTARY

The current Sound Lab includes three-long-blast sequences combined with one or two short blasts for entering/leaving harbour or tributary situations, plus three long blasts for the crossing signal taught there.
REDUCED VISIBILITY
Reduced-visibility signals are time-critical safety information. The Sound Lab includes repeated long-blast and ferry patterns; learn the sound and the operating context together.
RADIOTELEPHONY

Radio is part of inland navigation, but the applicable channel and procedure depend on the waterway and service. Establish the local arrangements before reaching a lock, bridge, port or reporting point.
RADIO DISCIPLINE

Listen before transmitting, identify the correct service/channel and keep calls relevant to safe navigation. A radio exchange supplements the navigation picture; it does not cancel the need for lookout and compliance with signals.
AUDIO PRACTICE

Use Sound Lab with the screen partly covered: hear the pattern first, identify it from sound alone, then reveal the label. That turns the horn library into recognition training rather than a sound-effects page.

modules.title: Rules of the Road
modules.desc: Apply inland conduct rules to traffic constrained by fairways, banks, signs and infrastructure.
sections: CONSTRAINED TRAFFIC
Inland encounters happen inside a physical system: channel edges, bends, bridges, locks, shoals, moorings and commercial traffic can all limit the manoeuvres available to you.
LOOKOUT FIRST

Maintain an effective lookout and build the traffic picture before deciding what rule or local instruction applies. Electronics are additional information, not a substitute for observing the waterway.
FAIRWAY THINKING

Know where the navigable fairway lies and how much room your vessel actually needs. A manoeuvre that looks simple on a screen may be impossible once depth, width or another vessel’s dimensions are considered.
MEETING
When vessels meet, determine the applicable inland rule and any signs, local traffic arrangement or agreed procedure early. Avoid forcing a close-quarters decision at a bend or restriction.
OVERTAKING

Overtaking requires enough room, time and knowledge of the other vessel and waterway. A prohibition such as A.2 ends the question: do not treat an apparently clear screen as permission to ignore the sign.
CROSSING / JOINING

Entering, leaving or crossing a main waterway can involve specific signs and traffic responsibilities. Establish the local situation before moving from a harbour, tributary or side channel into established traffic.
BENDS AND BLIND SECTIONS
Reduced sight lines increase the value of early speed control, correct position, sound/radio procedure where applicable and anticipation of commercial traffic that may occupy substantial width.
SPEED AND WASH
Safe speed inland is about more than collision avoidance. Banks, moored craft, works, restricted visibility and local limits can all require earlier reduction of speed and careful wash management.
COMMERCIAL TRAFFIC

Large inland vessels and formations may have limited manoeuvring options and significant dimensions. Do not create a situation where your small craft relies on another vessel making an impossible last-second move.
DECISION ORDER
Lookout → waterway constraint → vessel/traffic status → signs and signals → local instructions → early clear action → monitor the result. Reassess whenever the picture changes.

modules.title: Bridges, Locks, Berthing & Operations
modules.desc: Prepare for infrastructure before your manoeuvring choices disappear.
sections: LOCK PREPARATION
Before arrival, establish the lock’s operating instructions, opening information, traffic signals, radio/reporting procedure, waiting area and any requirements relevant to your vessel.
WAITING POSITION
Do not drift into a lock approach simply because the chamber looks available. Know where to wait and keep clear of traffic that has been instructed to enter or leave.
TRAFFIC SIGNALS
Lock and bridge lights/signals are operating instructions. Read the complete display and obey the applicable local procedure rather than relying on what another vessel appears to be doing.
IN THE LOCK
Prepare lines, fenders and crew before entry. Maintain control as water level changes and follow the lock keeper/local instructions. The safe setup depends on the vessel and the installation.
BRIDGE OPENINGS
Identify the correct usable opening before committing. D.1 in the verified sign library marks a recommended opening; other signs or signals may impose different restrictions or instructions.
HEADROOM

Air draught and available headroom must be considered together. Allow for the actual vessel configuration and the applicable water-level/clearance information rather than assuming a nominal figure is automatically safe.
OVERHEAD CABLES
E.2 identifies an overhead cable crossing. Treat aerial obstructions as a real clearance problem, especially where masts, aerials or other equipment increase your effective air draught.
BERTHING
Berthing can be permitted, prohibited or restricted by signs and local rules. A physically convenient wall, bank or quay is not automatically a legal or safe place to stop.
ANCHORING

Apply the same discipline to anchoring: check the signs, local restrictions, traffic needs and physical suitability. Never obstruct a fairway or controlled approach because the holding ground looks convenient.
SPECIAL OPERATIONS
Works, dredging, diving, ferries and other operations can alter the normal traffic picture. Identify their displayed signals and follow temporary or local directions around the operation.

modules.title: Radar, Inland AIS & Reporting
modules.desc: Use electronic information as part of the picture without surrendering judgement to the screen.
sections: WHAT AIS GIVES YOU
Inland AIS can provide transmitted identification, position and other data. It is valuable situational information, but it only contains what is transmitted and correctly received.
WHAT AIS CANNOT PROMISE
AIS does not guarantee another vessel’s intentions, manoeuvre or compliance. It does not create right of way and should never be used as permission to stop looking outside.
VISUAL CROSS-CHECK
Compare AIS with the vessel you can see, its aspect, lights/shapes, actual movement and the waterway. A mismatch is a reason to investigate, not a reason to force reality to fit the screen.
RADAR

Radar can extend awareness, particularly when visibility is reduced, but correct use requires understanding of the equipment, presentation and local/rule requirements. It is not an automatic collision-avoidance answer.
REDUCED VISIBILITY
In poor visibility, slow the situation down. Apply the relevant sound, radio and navigation requirements, maintain an effective lookout and avoid allowing electronic confidence to increase risk.
REPORTING POINTS
Some waterways or controlled sections require reports. Know what point triggers the report, which service/channel is used and what information is expected before you arrive there.
LOCK / PORT COMMUNICATION

Calls to locks, ports or traffic services should be made on the applicable local channel and according to the local procedure. Do not invent a procedure because it resembles a marina you already know.
DATA CONFLICT
If AIS, radar, chart and visual information disagree, identify which inputs could be stale, misidentified or misunderstood. Maintain safe margins while you verify.
ELECTRONIC DISCIPLINE
Set up displays before the workload peaks. Useful electronics reduce workload only when the navigator understands what each source can and cannot establish.
HUMAN DECISION
The skipper remains responsible for interpreting the complete situation. Project Watch deliberately tests electronic information alongside visual and rule-based evidence, not in isolation.

modules.title: Environment, Emergencies & Passage Readiness
modules.desc: Turn the rules into a complete, repeatable inland passage routine.
sections: ENVIRONMENTAL DUTY
Prevention of water pollution and disposal of waste sit within the CEVNI framework. Inland seamanship includes protecting the waterway as well as navigating through it.
WASTE
Plan waste handling rather than improvising it underway. Use the applicable reception/disposal arrangements and comply with the rules applying to the vessel and waterway.
SPILLS
Prevent fuel, oil and other pollutants reaching the water. If an incident occurs, prioritise safety, limit further release where it can be done safely and follow the applicable reporting procedure.
URGENT WARNING
Recognise the danger sound vocabulary before you need it. At least six very short blasts is an urgent collision-danger warning in the material taught by Sound Lab.
LOSS OF MANOEUVRABILITY
In constrained water, a propulsion or steering problem can become serious quickly. Keep escape options, avoid unnecessary close approaches and know how to communicate the developing hazard.
INCIDENT REPORTING
Know how the competent authority expects incidents and hazards to be reported on the waterway you are using. The correct contact/procedure is part of passage preparation.
PASSAGE DIMENSIONS
Before departure confirm draught, beam and air-draught requirements against known restrictions, locks, bridges and the information currently applicable to the route.
PASSAGE INFORMATION
Check notices, closures, works, waterway restrictions, lock/bridge operation, radio channels, reporting requirements and relevant weather/current/water-level information.
CREW PREPARATION

Brief the crew on lines, fenders, locks, waiting positions, radio responsibilities and what happens if the plan changes. Constrained manoeuvres improve when everyone knows the next job before it begins.
FALLBACK PLAN
For each critical section ask: where can I safely wait, turn, stop or abort? A fallback decided early is far more useful than one invented after the vessel is committed.
FINAL READINESS LOOP
Rules → notices → vessel dimensions → route restrictions → signs/marking → sound/radio → locks/bridges → traffic → environment → fallback. Then keep updating the picture underway.
ASSESSMENT GATE
Only after the teaching, visual recognition, Sound Lab and Practical work should the 30-question mock be used as a knowledge check. It remains independent training, not an official CEVNI examination.
